items.title: The Hundred Years War lasted 116 years
items.claim: When did the Hundred Years War begin and end?

options.text: 1337 (Edward III claims the French throne) to 1453 (Battle of Castillon) — 116 years, with long truces in between

items.reveal_title: A name invented in the 19th century
items.reveal:
The phrase 'Hundred Years War' was coined by French historians in the 1860s. Contemporaries did not see it as a single conflict but as a series of campaigns separated by long peaces (e.g. the Treaty of Brétigny, 1360).

Major English victories: Crécy (1346), Poitiers (1356), Agincourt (1415). Major French recoveries: Du Guesclin's reconquests under Charles V, and Joan of Arc's relief of Orléans (1429). It ended with the French victory at Castillon in 1453 — three months before Constantinople fell.
items.why: Periodisation is a historical choice, not a fact. A '100 years' war that was actually 116, mostly truce, and named four centuries later is a useful reminder.

items.title: British smallpox vaccination became compulsory in 1853
items.claim: When did vaccination become compulsory in the UK?

options.text: The Vaccination Act 1853 made infant smallpox vaccination compulsory in England and Wales; the 1867 Act introduced fines for non-compliance; the 1898 Act allowed a 'conscientious objection' exemption after mass protest
It was made compulsory only in 1948

items.reveal:
Edward Jenner published his cowpox technique in 1798. The 1853 Vaccination Act required parents to vaccinate infants within three months of birth, or face fines. The 1867 Act added imprisonment for repeated refusal.

The Leicester Anti-Vaccination League (founded 1869) led mass protest; in 1885, around 100,000 marched in Leicester against the Act. The 'Leicester method' substituted isolation and sanitation for compulsory vaccination — and Leicester's smallpox mortality remained low.

The 1898 Act introduced 'conscientious objection' as a legal category. Smallpox was declared eradicated globally by WHO on 8 May 1980 — the only human disease ever eradicated.
items.why: Public health enforcement has always provoked opposition. The 19th-century vaccination debate created the legal category of 'conscientious objection' — a concept later used for military service and other state requirements.

items.title: Children under 10 worked underground in British coal mines until 1842
items.claim: What did the Mines Act of 1842 prohibit?

options.text: All child labour in the UK
Underground employment for women and girls, and for boys under 10 — following Lord Ashley's (later Shaftesbury) commission report with illustrations of children pulling coal trucks
Coal mining itself, switching the country to oil

items.reveal:
The 1842 Royal Commission report on children in mines included engravings of half-naked children — boys as young as 5 acting as 'trappers' opening ventilation doors, girls and women hauling coal in chains. The illustrations shocked Parliament.

The Act banned women and girls underground entirely and boys under 10. Earlier factory legislation (1819, 1833, 1844) limited child working hours and required schooling. Robert Owen's New Lanark mills (from 1800) had already shown a different model.
items.why: 'Reform' was driven partly by humanitarian shock and partly by middle-class anxiety about working-class women. The Acts solved one problem (underground child labour) without addressing others (above-ground work continued for decades).
